name: CES Helm Simulator
summary: Boat-helm exhibit for CES 2026. I built the UI architecture and live sync with the sim and real helm.
subtitle: A real-time boat-helm simulator for Brunswick’s CES 2026 exhibit, driven by a real helm.

video.caption: Promo footage of the CES 2026 exhibit

problem.heading: Two separate projects had to feel like one boat.
problem.body: The exhibit paired an Unreal environment (boat, water, world) with a separate Unreal dashboard and 3D map, both driven by a real helm. Every turn of the wheel had to land in both at once, while a team of interns kept shipping new screens. This was the exhibit’s third iteration; I’d worked on versions since 2023.

highlights.heading: Three pieces that held it together

items.title: A UI architecture that made screens fast to build
items.challenge: Every dashboard screen was wired by hand, so each new view rebuilt the same plumbing and took about two weeks.
items.approach: I rebuilt the dashboard on CommonUI with MVVM. View models hold the live data (speed, heading, steering, weather, distance) and screens just bind to them, while CommonUI handles stacking and input focus.
items.result: New screens dropped from 2 weeks to 3–4 days, and the intern I mentored could build screens by binding to existing view models.

visual.caption: Helm and game events → view models → bound widgets.

items.title: One event stream, two projects
items.challenge: The UI and environment were separate projects built by different people, so the map, gauges and world drifted out of sync.
items.approach: I designed and documented the WebSocket events that pass state between them in week one, then debugged the 3D map (another intern’s task) and linked it to those events.
items.result: The dashboard, map and world moved together as one experience.

visual.caption: Helm → CAN bus → environment ↔ WebSocket events ↔ UI and 3D map (redrawn).

items.title: A dashboard that feels alive
items.challenge: The gauges had to reflect the actual helm, and a dashboard showing only speed felt static.
items.approach: I learned to read the helm’s CAN bus data and fed speed, direction and steering angle into the view models, then added simulated weather, time of day, and distance traveled from in-game speed.
items.result: The gauges responded to the real wheel and throttle, and the dashboard told the story of a trip.

visual.caption: Dashboard with helm-driven and simulated data called out.

stats.label: per UI screen, down from 2 weeks
live, driven by a real helm

reflection.worked: Agreeing on the WebSocket event schema in week one and documenting it. Two projects were built in parallel and still plugged together, and MVVM let that live data flow straight into the screens.
reflection.differently: Turn the UI into a reusable base. We started by copying files from the 2025 version; a base project or UI plugin would make the next exhibit a setup step instead of a cleanup.

name: Fliteboard Simulator
summary: An eFoil simulator I rebuilt: real thrust physics, a race mode with rider summaries, new controls.
subtitle: An eFoil ride experience for Brunswick, rebuilt with real physics, a race mode and new controls.

role.detail: Owned the project after inheriting it

outcome.detail: Each left with a personal ride summary

video.caption: Promo footage of the Fliteboard experience

problem.heading: An inherited simulator held together by magic numbers.
problem.body: Board movement came from hand-tuned constants, the UI couldn’t track more than one rider, and the Bluetooth controller only worked through a script running outside the game. Brunswick wanted a competitive race mode with a takeaway for every rider.

items.title: From magic numbers to real thrust
items.challenge: Motion came from hand-tuned constants, so changing one thing broke how everything felt.
items.approach: I rewrote the movement with vector math and a simple thrust model, so speed and direction come from forces instead of magic numbers.
items.result: Predictable, tunable handling that carried two new level sections and a new board model for race mode.

visual.caption: Forces on the board: thrust, drag and lift.

items.title: Every rider leaves with their run
items.challenge: Race mode had to track several riders and give each one a personal summary.
items.approach: I rebuilt the UI on the CommonUI and MVVM base from CES Helm. Each run records route, board tilt, speed and controller thrust and exports it for the mailing list; a registration app gives every attendee a unique ID and sends their name into the game.
items.result: A summary screen for every rider, and follow-up data for 100–200 riders a day.

visual.caption: End-of-ride summary: route, tilt, speed and thrust.

items.title: Prototyping how you ride it
items.challenge: The real controller relied on an external script, and the team wanted to test riding by shifting your weight.
items.approach: I moved the Bluetooth C# integration into Unreal and prototyped weight control with force-sensitive pads, detecting which side had pressure with a slight linear curve. I also tried exposing the microcontroller as a gamepad, but it lacked XInput support.
items.result: Executives liked the weight prototype but chose camera controls for reliability, which my manager built into a unified input system.

reflection.worked: Replacing magic numbers with a real force model first. Every later addition (new levels, a new board, race mode) became easier to tune.
reflection.differently: Check hardware capabilities before committing. The gamepad plan stalled on the microcontroller’s missing XInput support, which a quick spike would have caught.

name: Echoes of the Elements
summary: Four-realm elemental game. I built the ability, save and UI systems, and brought in the hero.
subtitle: A third-person elemental adventure built by a team of four for CS 415: Game Development.

outcome.value: All 4 realms in a packaged build

video.caption: Gameplay capture from the packaged build

problem.heading: Four people, four realms, one game that has to feel like one game.
problem.body: Each teammate owned a realm (Earth, Air, Water, Fire), but every realm needed the same player, abilities, checkpoints and progress tracking. Without shared systems, we’d have shipped four games stitched together.

items.title: An ability system teammates could plug into
items.challenge: Abilities had to hit enemies, hazards and objects built by three other people, without everyone’s Blueprints depending on each other.
items.approach: One modular Ability Component holds mana, cooldowns and spawning; damage flows through a shared Character Interface, so anything with Receive Damage can be hit. On top: Fire Bolt, Flame Strike, a mana-draining Water Shield, double jump and air dash, plus templates for new enemy types.
items.result: Teammates’ enemies and hazards worked with every ability without touching my code. Combos were cut for time, but the hooks are there.

items.title: Progress that survives every level change
items.challenge: Moving between the hub and four realms reloads the level and wipes the player’s state.
items.approach: A persistent Game Instance tracks finished realms, and a Save Game stores health, mana, the last checkpoint and items. Checkpoints save on overlap, hub doors unlock from the completed list, and menus run on a CommonUI widget stack.
items.result: Clear a realm and the next portal opens; die, and you resume at your last checkpoint.

items.title: A playable hero on a student timeline
items.challenge: We needed a main character with a full moveset, but nobody had time to model and animate one from scratch.
items.approach: I generated the base model with Meshy AI, cleaned up geometry and fixed textures in Blender, retargeted free marketplace animations onto the new skeleton, and built ability effect meshes timed to my ability code.
items.result: A rigged, animated hero with matching effects in every realm.

visual.caption: The model before and after cleanup.

reflection.worked: Interface-driven damage. Building against “anything that can receive damage” let four people work in parallel without breaking each other’s levels.
reflection.differently: Scope down earlier. Combos and a final boss never made it, and the Air realm ended up least polished. I’d lock a smaller core loop first and treat extras as stretch goals.

name: CAD Simplifier
summary: Desktop tool that turns weeks of CAD remodeling into minutes: 7.4M → 27K triangles.
subtitle: Turning engineering CAD into real-time assets for boat simulation.

outcome.detail: 7.4M → 27K triangles on a Sea Ray SLX 280

video.caption: Before and after: the Sea Ray SLX 280 hull

problem.heading: Engineering CAD is built to manufacture a boat, not to render one at 60 fps.
problem.body: Boat CAD models every bolt, bracket and interior part. Exported, one hull runs to millions of triangles with overlapping, non-manifold geometry, and an artist spent weeks remodeling each boat by hand. I built this as an exploratory project while CES Helm was still in ideation.

items.title: Wrap first, decimate second
items.challenge: Decimating raw CAD directly collapses thin parts, keeps hidden interior geometry and leaves messy topology.
items.approach: I wrote a small C++ tool on CGAL’s 3D Alpha Wrapping that shrink-wraps the model in a clean, watertight surface. Alpha and offset scale with the model’s size, and a second, coarser pass tightens it further.
items.result: 7,374,479 → 1,260,118 → 410,694 triangles from the wraps, then 26,938 after Blender decimation.

items.title: Three tools, one button
items.challenge: The pipeline spans FreeCAD, a compiled C++ binary and Blender, each with its own command line and install location.
items.approach: A Python orchestrator runs each step as a subprocess and finds the installs automatically; headless Blender converts to quads, decimates and exports FBX; a Toga app exposes three sliders and a live log, packaged as a native installer.
items.result: The sim’s graphics team went from weeks of remodeling to minutes, and spent that time retexturing instead.

stats.label: not weeks, to a sim-ready hull

reflection.worked: Making alpha and offset relative to the model’s size, so one set of defaults worked across very different models.
reflection.differently: Plan for distribution and fidelity from the start. GPL components kept it internal; next I’d explore cleaner topology and preserving UV and texture data, so artists start closer to final.

name: Patito’s Patisserie
summary: Brand, duck and bilingual storefront for a cookie shop, with an admin the owner runs alone.
subtitle: A brand, a duck and a bilingual storefront for a small-batch Mexican-inspired cookie shop.

outcome.detail: No developer needed for weekly updates

video.caption: Walkthrough of the live storefront, in English and Spanish

problem.heading: A bakery whose menu changes every Friday can’t wait on a developer.
problem.body: Patito’s sells small-batch, Mexican-inspired cookies (horchata, Abuelita hot chocolate, churro) baked to order, with a new batch every Friday. The owner needed a site that felt like the brand, worked in English and Spanish, and could change week to week without anyone touching code.

highlights.heading: A brand and the tools to run it

items.title: A brand built around one duck
items.challenge: A small home bakery needed to feel warm, specific and memorable, not like a template.
items.approach: I designed the identity from scratch: Patito the duck in a chef’s hat, a four-color palette (deep green, sage, coral, sunny yellow), playful display type and a friendly bilingual voice.
items.result: One consistent personality across the logo, mascot, site and copy.

visual.caption: Brand sheet: the duck, palette swatches, type and a couple of site sections.

items.title: An owner who never needs a programmer
items.challenge: The menu changes weekly, and the owner wanted to tweak the look too, but isn’t a developer.
items.approach: The menu and design settings live in a Cloudflare D1 database behind an admin page. The storefront reads the menu from a Worker API (/api/menu) and is styled from design tokens, all on Cloudflare’s edge.
items.result: Menu updates and design tweaks go live with no code and no deploy.

visual.caption: The admin screen next to the storefront, showing an edit reflected live.

reflection.worked: Building the site on design tokens from day one. It’s what made “the owner can change the look” a simple feature instead of a rewrite.
reflection.differently: Validate the business before building the full platform. The bakery didn’t move past the idea stage, so I’d launch a simple menu page and order form first, and add the platform once orders came in.

name: Mix Space
summary: Room playlist built from everyone’s Spotify, matched to the host’s vibe by a local LLM.
subtitle: A crowd-sourced playlist for shared spaces, built in one evening at the Research Park Hackathon.

outcome.detail: Real listeners’ tracks queued from one prompt

video.caption: Recreated offline demo: prompt → matched playlist

problem.heading: Public spaces play one person’s playlist to a room full of people.
problem.body: Gyms, cafés and shops pick a playlist and hope. Mix Space lets everyone in the room shape it without installing anything: scan a code, log in with Spotify, and your top tracks join the pool. The host sets the mood in plain words, like “hype workout” or “coffeehouse acoustics.”

highlights.heading: Where the AI did the work

items.title: Teaching the playlist what a “vibe” is
items.challenge: A host types “chill coffeehouse,” but Spotify only hands back titles and artists. Nothing in that data says what a song feels like.
items.approach: For every pooled song, a local LLM writes a short description of its mood, genre and energy. I embedded those with a sentence-transformer and indexed them in Haystack, so the prompt runs as a semantic search for the top 10 matches.
items.result: Free-form prompts pulled sensible songs from a pool of 90 tracks across 6 listeners.

visual.caption: A prompt → the generated descriptions → the matched queue.

items.title: Picking the right model in a six-hour window
items.challenge: The search is only as good as the descriptions. Vague ones made every song look like every other song.
items.approach: I started with Gemma, compared its descriptions against Llama 3 on the same tracks, and switched to Llama 3 for its more specific mood and genre language. Both ran locally through Ollama, so there were no rate limits or API costs.
items.result: Clearer descriptions, so prompts and songs actually lined up.

visual.caption: One song’s Gemma description next to its Llama 3 description.

reflection.worked: Using an LLM to describe songs rather than classify them. It gave the search something meaningful to match, and the host could type any prompt.
reflection.differently: Record the demo the moment it works. Ours ran live, but the submitted video didn’t capture it, and Spotify has since closed its API to most new developers.

name: Wireless Sensing
summary: Handheld Pi that hunts a hidden camera by mapping Wi-Fi signal strength against footsteps.
subtitle: Finding a hidden spy camera with packet sniffing and step tracking, for the CS 437 Midterm Competition.

problem.heading: A camera is hidden in the room. All you have is its Wi-Fi traffic.
problem.body: A Raspberry Pi “spy camera” was hidden somewhere in a zoned room. We had to find it with our own Pi, using only the signal strength (RSSI) of its packets and the Sense HAT’s motion sensors. On Day 2 the camera only transmitted when it detected motion, and decoys were added.

items.title: Turning footsteps into a signal map
items.challenge: IMU data was too noisy to double-integrate into a position, especially once we stopped walking in a straight line.
items.approach: We sniffed only the camera’s packets in monitor mode with Scapy, logging RSSI with each accelerometer reading, and pressed the joystick at every turn to stamp direction. A Savitzky-Golay filter smoothed the signal; peaks became steps, and a stride estimate turned steps into distance.
items.result: A walked path colored by RSSI. On Day 1 the strongest signal pointed to the correct zone.

visual.caption: Day 1 RSSI-vs-position plot, plus raw vs. smoothed acceleration.

items.title: What Day 2 taught us
items.challenge: We got the zone wrong. Holding the Pi steady flattened the bounce step detection needs, we ran the Day 1 script by mistake, and packets arrived after I’d walked past the camera.
items.approach: We rebuilt the tool for real-time feedback: the Sense HAT’s LED shifts color as RSSI rises or falls against the best reading so far, and collection moved onto separate threads so no packets or steps were dropped.
items.result: A device you can steer by while walking, instead of one you can only read afterward.

visual.caption: The LED color scale, next to the Day 2 step plot.

reflection.worked: Using the joystick to record direction. It sidestepped the IMU’s worst weakness and made step-based tracking workable.
reflection.differently: Design for feedback during the search, not just analysis after it, and rehearse the exact run. Our best idea for Day 2 sat unused because we launched the wrong script.

name: AJO
summary: Gesture-controlled mobile platformer. I concepted Ajo and painted every elemental power.
subtitle: A gesture-controlled mobile platformer built in two weeks at the National High School Game Academy, Carnegie Mellon.

outcome.detail: Pitch to final demo in 2 weeks

video.caption: Gameplay capture from the final build

problem.heading: Two weeks to turn a pitch into a game nobody had seen before.
problem.body: Faculty formed new teams to build original games. We pitched three ideas and they picked AJO: a puzzle platformer where Ajo, a boy who lost his memory, recovers it level by level. Every power is cast by drawing a shape: swipe for Wind, circle for Fire, triangle for Earth, rectangle for Water.

items.title: Wind, the power that changes with the world
items.challenge: Wind is AJO’s core power, used to move yourself and objects. It needed a different look in each level while staying instantly recognizable.
items.approach: I painted the wind effects and their level-specific variations in Photoshop, then worked with the programmers on the logic that picks the right animation for the current level.
items.result: One wind power, with the right version showing up in every level.

visual.caption: The wind variations side by side, plus a clip of it in play.

items.title: When a triangle looks like a circle
items.challenge: Earth is cast by drawing a triangle, but quick, rounded triangles kept being read as circles, which cast Fire instead.
items.approach: I worked with the programmers to tune the recognizer’s corner detection, adjusting the angle threshold that decides whether a turn in the stroke counts as a corner.
items.result: Sloppy triangles still register three corners and reliably cast the Earth rock.

visual.caption: A drawn triangle with its detected corners marked, next to a circle.

reflection.worked: Implementing my own art in Unity and staying in the loop with the programmers. Most of the bugs I helped fix sat right where art met code.
reflection.differently: It was our first game, so: playtest with peers, not just our team; keep Perforce organized (I was often on an outdated version); and split assets with a shared style reference, since our two art styles didn’t always look cohesive.
